gloss: Mount Olympus in the north of Greece. Like Mount Helicon in Bœotia, it was a resort of the Muses to whom classical poets appealed for inspiration. Hence lines 3, 4 are a figurative way of claiming loftier inspiration than that of classical poets.
The allusion is to Proverbs viii. 23–30, where the word rendered “rejoicing” in verse 30 may mean ‘playing’ (*ludens* in the Vulgate); cf. “didst play,” 10.

an allusion to the legend that Bellerophon attempted to ascend to heaven on the back of Pegasus, but was flung to the ground. Incurring the anger of the gods, he roamed alone in the Aleian plain, ‘the land of wandering,’ became distracted and died; cf. Homer, *Iliad* VI. 200–202.
i.e. “the Astronomical Universe of Man, which appears to revolve round the Earth daily in twenty-four hours” (Masson).
M. had many bitter enemies among the Royalist party; as was only natural considering the attitude which he had adopted towards Charles I. in *The Tenure of Kings* and *Eikonoklastes*.
*darkness*, i.e. blindness. *dangers*. At the Restoration M. was arrested and imprisoned for some months, probably from August to December 1660, for having defended the execution of Charles I.

Cf. the similar allusion in *Lycidas*, 58–63, to the classical legend that Orpheus was torn to pieces, and his head thrown into the river Hebrus, by Thracian women in their Bacchanalian orgies, his mother Calliope, the Muse of epic poetry, being unable to do aught for his defence.
no doubt M. intends a comparison between the “wild rout” (a contemptuous word) of Bacchanals and the dissolute court of Charles II., and perhaps hints that he himself may suffer like Orpheus.
probably M. in depicting Raphael thus as a power friendly to man is thinking of the story in the Apocryphal Book of Tobit how the archangel befriended Tobias.
expounder, explainer; cf. *Interpres divum* (said of Mercury), *Aeneid* IV. 378.
was completed; Lat. *absolvere*, ‘to finish.’
i.e. “though he has passed the meridian and is now on his descent, *pronus*” (Keightley). The standing-still of the sun was probably suggested by Joshua x. 12–14.
Hesperus; the classical name of the planet Venus when it appeared after sunset; seen before sunrise, it was called “Lucifer.”
*inventions*, thoughts, foolish imaginations; cf. its use in Psalm cvi. 29. *hope*, hope for, i.e. to know. Elizabethans use *hope* transitively.

the name Lucifer, ‘light-bringer,’ is properly a Latin title of the morning-star, but it was applied by patristic writers to Satan, in allusion perhaps to the tradition of the original “brightness” of his person. Milton says that “Lucifer” and “Satan” were the names given to the arch-rebel after his expulsion from Heaven.
an absolute construction; cf. “him destroyed,” IX. 130. In Shakespeare, as now, the absolute case is the nominative; but in older English it was the dative.
dwell at ease (having vanquished the rebels). Some explain ‘dwell at large’ (cf. Lat. *habitare laxe*), as though the expulsion of the rebels gave the others more room in Heaven.

“There are no limits to Chaos, because I who fill it am infinite; and it is not vacuous or empty, because I am everywhere in it, though I only exhibit my goodness in a limited space, i.e. in Heaven” (Keightley’s note).
“The Lord hath opened his armoury,” Jeremiah l. 25. The sword with which Michael overcame Satan in the great battle in Heaven was “from the armoury of God” (VI. 321).

lemma: with the centre mix the pole
gloss: Richardson explains: “There was such confusion in Chaos, as if on earth the sea in mountainous waves should rise from its very bottom to assault Heaven (i.e. the sky), and mix the centre of the globe with the extremities of it.”
cf. Proverbs viii. 27, “When he prepared the heavens, I was there: when he set a compass upon the face of the depth.”
in *The Christian Doctrine*, I. 7, Milton explains that he understands this to mean, in this context, God’s “divine power, rather than any person” of the Trinity.

established and caused to coalesce. At first the Universe carved out of Chaos is a “fluid mass” (237) of “matter unformed” (233). Now atoms (*semina rerum*) of a like nature are brought together so as to form a solid substance.

partaking of the nature of ether. Properly *ether* means very bright atmosphere; light, therefore, may well be called ‘ethereal.’ Bacon speaks of the “four mutable elements and one immutable fifth Essence,” i.e. the “quintessence.”

there are “waters” in the Universe because Chaos, of which it was a portion, was a kind of sea. The “firmament,” according to M., is the expanse of air, stretching from the Earth to the Crystalline Sphere.
*genial*, creative, fertilising.
the whole picture is that of a great wave just before it breaks on the sea-shore.
Raphael had described to Adam in bk. VI. the contests in Heaven between the good Angels and the rebels.
cf. the comparison in IV. 980–83 between the bristling spears of an army and ears of corn. *humble*, low-growing; cf. Lat. *humilis* used of trees.
alternation, Lat. *vicissitudo*.
Venus; commonly called “Lucifer” as the morning-star and then treated as masculine.
“Canst thou bind the sweet influences of Pleiades?” Job xxxviii. 31. The Pleiades rise about the spring equinox, and, according to a common belief, the Creation took place in spring.
divided, Lat. *dividuus*: she shares her “reign” with the stars.
creeping things (*reptilia*). The term comprises fishes of all sorts. *soul*; used as a collective term = ‘creatures.’
the whale; cf. the similar description in I. 200–205.

i.e. cleave as with a wedge. He is thinking of the *cuneus* or ‘wedge’ of the Roman army, viz. the formation of troops into an acute angle, the point of which had to pierce into the massed forces of the enemy.
“After a little time the bird that forms the apex or point quits it and falls back, and another takes his place”—Keightley. Hence M. says “with mutual wing easing.”
an Elizabethan form of the word *leopard*, so called because thought to be a cross between a lion (*leo*) and a panther (*pardus*).
the elephant.
*parsimonious*, thrifty; used in a good sense. *emmet*; in origin the same word as *ant*. M. recollected Horace’s description of the ant—*haud ignara ac non incauta futuri* (*Satires* I. 1. 35).
Milton shows his republicanism.
it was a common belief of Milton’s time that the working-bees were female, the males being drones (so called from their droning buzz).

M. treats man’s “upright” (509) stature as a sign of his superiority to and authority over animals. One feels a suggestion of the old thought that the purpose of this “erection” of stature, peculiar to man, was “for to behold and look up toward heaven.”

in X. 210, 211 we read how the sentence passed upon Adam is relaxed, and “the instant stroke of death… removed,” so that after his sin he is still suffered by the Almighty to live, but no longer in Paradise.
in the famous allegory in II. 648–870 Sin is represented as the mother of Death. They are always in the poem introduced together, Death attending Sin as “her shadow” (IX. 12).

the Old Testament often speaks of Angels visiting the Earth, and in III. 529–37 M. says that there were two aerial paths for their descent, one leading straight down from Heaven on to Mount Sion, the other extending over the whole Promised Land.
‘the Milky way’; called *lacteae plagae* (‘the milky regions’) in Milton’s poem *In Obitum Praesulis Eliensis*, 60.

lemma: dulcimer, all organs of sweet stop
gloss: *dulcimer*, a stringed instrument, played with small hammers; probably of Babylonish origin. *all organs*, wind instruments, opposed to the stringed instruments in 597. Properly *stop* = ‘that by which the sounds of wind instruments are regulated’; hence = ‘tone, notes.’

a comparison is implied between the rebellious Angels and the Giants of classical mythology who sought to expel Zeus and the gods from Olympus. *thy thunders*; see the account of the battle in Heaven, VI. 834–66.
“the glassy sea” = the Crystalline Sphere. Milton, “when he uses Greek words, sometimes gives the English with them”—Newton.
M. refers more than once to the likelihood of the heavenly bodies being inhabited.
*O fortunatos nimium sua si bona norint*, Vergil, *Georg.* II. 458. *persevere*, remain steadfastly.
